questions.stem: A 39 year old hairdresser who has had three pregnancies has had aching, heavy legs for a year, worse at the end of a working day. When she stands, there are blue, dilated, tortuous veins along the inner side of her right calf and thigh. Both calves are soft and non-tender. Foot pulses are palpable. Her temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Visible dilated, tortuous veins along the medial calf and thigh with aching, heavy legs worse by evening in a woman with pregnancies and a standing job are varicose veins.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: worse at the end of a working day
dilated, tortuous veins along the inner side
steps.x: Classic long saphenous distribution with typical symptoms and risk factors.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Varicose veins.

elim: A popliteal swelling behind the knee.
Non-pitting swelling including the foot, without tortuous veins.
A hard, red, tender cord along a vein.

steps.x: **E. Varicose veins.** Tortuous medial leg veins + evening aching = varicose veins.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has had bulging veins on his left calf for 3 years with ankle swelling by the evening. The veins are tortuous and fill quickly from above when he stands after lying with the leg raised. Pulses are normal and his ABPI is 1.1. His BP is 132/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Varicose veins are caused by incompetent venous valves, leading to venous reflux and venous hypertension.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: tortuous and fill quickly from above
steps.x: Rapid filling from above means blood is flowing the wrong way.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Incompetent venous valves.

elim: Bilateral oedema and raised JVP, not focal varicosities.
Rare and present from childhood; his began at 47.

steps.x: **B. Incompetent venous valves.** Varicose veins = incompetent valves → reflux → venous hypertension.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman is 30 weeks pregnant with her third child. Over the past 2 months she has noticed new bulging, tortuous veins on the inner side of both calves, with aching by the evening. She does not smoke, has no medical history and her BMI before pregnancy was 22 kg/m². Her BP is 116/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason for her new veins?
questions.e: Pregnancy is a recognised risk factor for varicose veins, through raised venous pressure and hormonal relaxation of vein walls; obesity and standing occupation are others.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: 30 weeks pregnant with her third child
steps.x: Find the varicose vein risk factor in the stem.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pregnancy.

elim: Her BP is normal; an arterial risk factor.
She does not smoke; an arterial risk factor.
She has none; an arterial risk factor.

steps.x: **C. Pregnancy.** Varicose vein risk factors: obesity, pregnancy, standing occupation, prior DVT.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has new varicose veins of his right leg with brown skin above the ankle. He had a right femoral deep vein thrombosis after a knee operation 8 years ago. He works in an office, has a BMI of 24 kg/m² and has never been pregnant. His BP is 128/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which factor in his history most likely explains his varicose veins?
questions.e: Varicose veins typically affect middle-aged adults, sometimes after a previous DVT that damages valves and raises venous pressure.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: new varicose veins of his right leg
steps.x: Same leg, valve-damaging event.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Previous deep vein thrombosis.

elim: Not described and not a venous risk factor.
Sitting is less of a risk than standing jobs.
Not described and an arterial risk factor.

steps.x: **D. Previous deep vein thrombosis.** Prior DVT damages valves → varicose veins.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman who works from home has had aching, bulging veins in both legs for 2 years. She has no previous DVT and has never been pregnant. Her BMI is 38 kg/m². She does not smoke. On standing there are tortuous veins along both medial calves. Her BP is 136/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most important risk factor for her varicose veins?
questions.e: Obesity is the key risk factor for varicose veins, increasing intra-abdominal and venous pressure.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: tortuous veins along both medial calves
steps.x: No pregnancy, no DVT, not standing: what is left?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Obesity.

elim: Slightly more common in women, but much weaker than obesity.
Not a venous risk factor; BP is near normal.
Pregnancy, not nulliparity, is the risk.

steps.x: **D. Obesity.** Key risk factor: obesity.

questions.stem: A 52 year old nurse has visible tortuous veins along her right medial calf. She works 12-hour shifts on her feet. Her foot pulses are palpable and the calf is soft and non-tender. She has no ulcer. Her temperature is 36.6°C and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which symptom is she most likely to describe?
o: Calf cramp on walking relieved by rest
Constant burning pain in both feet at night
Heaviness and aching that worsen towards the end of the day
Pain eased by hanging the leg out of bed
Sudden severe calf pain with swelling
questions.e: Varicose veins give aching, heavy legs with swelling that worsens towards the end of the day as venous pressure builds on standing.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Venous symptoms build with standing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Heaviness and aching that worsen towards the end of the day.
**C. Heaviness and aching that worsen towards the end of the day.** Varicose veins: heavy, aching legs, worse by evening.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has aching legs and visible tortuous veins on his left medial calf. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and the GP wants to exclude arterial disease as a cause of the aching. The foot pulses are palpable. Investigations: left ABPI 1.02. His BP is 138/84 mmHg.

visual.title: Left ABPI
visual.caption: A normal ABPI (above 0.8) supports a venous cause.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his leg aching?
questions.e: A normal ABPI (above 0.8) with visible tortuous medial calf veins supports varicose veins as the cause, not arterial disease.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
ABPI normal: arteries are fine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Varicose veins.

elim: Back and buttock pain eased by sitting forward, not visible veins.

steps.x: **E. Varicose veins.** Normal ABPI (>0.8) supports varicose veins.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has varicose veins running from the dorsum of her left foot, in front of the medial malleolus, up the inner calf and thigh towards the groin. Duplex ultrasound is planned to look for reflux at the junction where this vein ends. Her BP is 126/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Into which vein does the affected vein drain?
questions.e: The great (long) saphenous vein runs from the dorsum of the foot, in front of the medial malleolus, up the medial leg and drains into the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: in front of the medial malleolus
inner calf and thigh towards the groin
steps.x: This is the great saphenous vein, the most commonly affected system.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Femoral vein.

elim: The GSV joins the femoral vein in the groin, well below the IVC.
Drains the posterolateral leg into the popliteal vein.

steps.x: **A. Femoral vein.** Great saphenous → femoral vein at the SFJ; small saphenous → popliteal vein.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has had varicose veins for 25 years. She now has patchy discolouration of the skin of both lower legs, worst just above the medial malleoli. The skin is not itchy, ulcerated or hard. Pulses are palpable and her ABPI is 1.0. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely appearance of the skin?
questions.e: Chronic venous hypertension damages capillaries, red cells leak out and their breakdown product haemosiderin deposits in the skin as brown pigmentation.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Long-standing venous hypertension in the gaiter area.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Brown pigmentation.

elim: Atrophie blanche can occur, but the commonest discolouration is brown haemosiderin.

steps.x: **A. Brown pigmentation.** Venous pigmentation = haemosiderin, brown.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with long-standing varicose veins has itchy, red, scaly and weeping skin over his left lower medial calf. The area is not hot and there is no fever. There is brown staining around it. His foot pulses are palpable. His temperature is 36.8°C and BP 136/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Contact dermatitis to a new cream
questions.e: Venous eczema is a complication of varicose veins: itchy, red, scaly, weeping skin in the gaiter area alongside other venous skin changes.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Eczematous change in the gaiter area of a venous leg.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Venous eczema.

elim: Hot, tender, spreading erythema with fever.
Well-demarcated silvery plaques on extensor surfaces.
Annular scaly rash with central clearing.

steps.x: **E. Venous eczema.** Varicose veins + itchy scaly gaiter skin = venous eczema.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman with varicose veins for 30 years has had a sore on her right leg for 3 months. It is shallow, with an irregular edge and a moist, granulating base, just above the medial malleolus. The surrounding skin is brown and hard. Pulses are palpable and her ABPI is 1.05.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Venous ulcers are a complication of varicose veins: shallow, irregular, moist ulcers above the medial malleolus with surrounding venous skin changes.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Gaiter area, irregular, wet, normal ABPI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Venous ulcer.

elim: Punched out, dry, distal, low ABPI.
Pearly rolled edge, usually sun-exposed face.
Over bony prominences in immobile patients.

steps.x: **E. Venous ulcer.** Varicose veins + medial malleolus shallow wet ulcer = venous ulcer.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with varicose veins of her right leg has had sudden, painful swelling of the whole right calf for 2 days after a long-haul flight. The calf is 4 cm larger than the left, tense and tender, and the pain is not limited to a visible vein. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which complication is most likely?
questions.e: Sudden painful swelling in a leg with varicose veins is an emergency feature suggesting DVT (or superficial thrombophlebitis if confined to a superficial vein).

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: sudden, painful swelling of the whole right calf
not limited to a visible vein
steps.x: Whole-calf swelling, not a single cord.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Deep vein thrombosis.

elim: Chronic woody induration, not acute swelling.
Possible, but there is no knee history and the flight points to DVT.

steps.x: **A. Deep vein thrombosis.** Sudden painful swelling in VV = think DVT or thrombophlebitis.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with varicose veins has a soft, bluish swelling in her right groin, inferior and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It is visible when she stands and disappears when she lies down. A thrill is felt on coughing and tapping over it. Her temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A saphena varix is dilation of the great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction, inferior and lateral to the pubic tubercle, with a bluish tinge that disappears lying down and a positive cough impulse.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: inferior and lateral to the pubic tubercle
steps.x: A varicose dilation where the GSV meets the femoral vein.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Saphena varix.

elim: Pulsatile and expansile, not bluish or vanishing lying down.
Also below and lateral to the tubercle with a cough impulse, but not blue, and it has no fluid thrill on tapping.
Firm nodes that do not disappear lying down.

steps.x: **E. Saphena varix.** Blue groin lump that vanishes lying down in a VV patient = saphena varix.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has had varicose veins for 20 years. His lower calves have narrowed above the ankles while the upper calves remain full, like an upside-down bottle. The skin there is brown. His pulses are palpable and his ABPI is 1.1. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on palpation of the lower calf?
questions.e: Lipodermatosclerosis is progressive fibrosis of the skin and subcutaneous fat from chronic venous hypertension, giving hard, woody induration.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Inverted champagne bottle leg = lipodermatosclerosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hard, woody induration.

elim: Earlier venous change; fibrosis makes the skin hard.

steps.x: **B. Hard, woody induration.** Lipodermatosclerosis = woody fibrotic induration.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has varicose veins of her left leg. She asks whether she needs a specialist. Over the last month she has had two episodes of a vein on her ankle bleeding heavily after a minor knock. She also mentions mild aching and some thread veins. Her BP is 128/78 mmHg and Hb is 128 g/L.
questions.q: Which feature is the clearest indication for referral to vascular surgery?
o: Varicose veins on one leg only
questions.e: Referral criteria for varicose veins are bleeding, pain, superficial thrombophlebitis, ulceration and severe impact on quality of life.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: two episodes of a vein on her ankle bleeding heavily
steps.x: Which feature is on the referral list?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bleeding from a varicose vein.

elim: Pain counts when significant, but bleeding is the clearer indication.

steps.x: **B. Bleeding from a varicose vein.** Refer for bleeding, pain, thrombophlebitis, ulceration or severe QoL impact.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman had surgery for varicose veins of her right leg 6 years ago. She now has new bulging veins along her medial thigh and calf with aching and evening swelling that affect her work. She has been referred to a vascular clinic to plan treatment. Her ABPI is 1.1.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Duplex venous ultrasound is the gold standard, showing venous reflux and valve incompetence and mapping which veins to treat.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: new bulging veins along her medial thigh and calf
steps.x: Recurrent varicose veins needing a treatment map.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Duplex venous ultrasound.

elim: Used for pelvic or central veins, not routine assessment.
An outdated bedside test, now replaced by duplex.

steps.x: **C. Duplex venous ultrasound.** Gold standard = duplex venous ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man has tortuous varicose veins along his left medial calf and thigh with aching by evening. Duplex venous ultrasound of the left leg is performed with him standing, and the calf is squeezed and released while the sonographer watches the groin.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding?
o: Absent flow in the femoral vein
Normal flow towards the heart only
questions.e: Duplex shows venous reflux and valve incompetence: in great saphenous varicose veins, blood flows back down through the incompetent saphenofemoral junction.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: varicose veins along his left medial calf and thigh
steps.x: GSV varicose veins come from an incompetent SFJ.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reflux at the saphenofemoral junction.

elim: An arterial finding; duplex here studies veins.

steps.x: **D. Reflux at the saphenofemoral junction.** Duplex in varicose veins shows reflux and valve incompetence.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with symptomatic varicose veins is unfit for any intervention. The GP would like to prescribe compression stockings. He has type 2 diabetes, smokes and has calf pain on walking 100 metres. Dorsalis pedis pulses are faint. His BP is 146/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which investigation must be done before the stockings are prescribed?
questions.e: ABPI must be checked before compression: stockings are contraindicated if ABPI is below 0.8 because compression can worsen ischaemia in arterial disease.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Possible coexisting PAD: check arteries before compressing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ankle-brachial pressure index.

elim: Maps reflux for intervention, which he is not having.
Does not decide safety of compression.

steps.x: **A. Ankle-brachial pressure index.** Always ABPI before compression.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with symptomatic varicose veins is not fit for intervention and wants compression stockings. She has hypertension and an ex-smoker's history. The practice nurse measures her right ankle systolic pressure at 84 mmHg and brachial systolic pressure at 140 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: ABPI 0.6: arterial disease, so compression stockings are contraindicated
ABPI 0.6: normal, so stockings are safe
ABPI 0.6: venous disease, so stockings are needed
ABPI 0.9: borderline, so stockings are safe
questions.e: ABPI = 84/140 = 0.6; below 0.8 indicates peripheral arterial disease, and compression could worsen ischaemia.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
84 divided by 140 = 0.6.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ABPI 0.6: arterial disease, so compression stockings are contraindicated.

elim: The ratio is ankle over brachial.

steps.x: **A. ABPI 0.6: arterial disease, so compression stockings are contraindicated.** ABPI below 0.8 = no compression.

questions.stem: A 41 year old teacher has painful varicose veins on her right medial thigh and calf that limit her work. She has had one episode of superficial thrombophlebitis. She is keen on endothermal ablation. Her pulses are normal. Her BP is 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which investigation is needed before treatment can be planned?
questions.e: Duplex venous ultrasound confirms the diagnosis, demonstrates reflux and valve incompetence and maps veins before endothermal ablation.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Before any intervention, map the reflux.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Duplex venous ultrasound.

elim: Not routine for leg varicose veins.
Not indicated after a single superficial thrombophlebitis.

steps.x: **B. Duplex venous ultrasound.** Before intervention = duplex.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has mild aching from varicose veins of his left calf. There is no bleeding, ulceration, skin change or thrombophlebitis. His BMI is 33 kg/m² and he takes little exercise. He wants to avoid any procedure. His ABPI is 1.1 and BP 134/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Leg elevation, weight loss and exercise
questions.e: First-line management is conservative: leg elevation, weight loss and exercise.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.

clues: no bleeding, ulceration, skin change or thrombophlebitis
steps.x: Uncomplicated veins, obesity, no wish for intervention.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Leg elevation, weight loss and exercise.

elim: For symptomatic patients who want intervention.

steps.x: **B. Leg elevation, weight loss and exercise.** First-line: elevate, lose weight, exercise.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman has symptomatic varicose veins with aching and evening swelling. She has severe heart failure and is unsuitable for any interventional treatment. Her foot pulses are palpable and her ABPI is 1.05. She already elevates her legs. Her BP is 118/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management for symptom relief?
questions.e: Compression stockings are used for symptomatic relief when interventional treatment is unsuitable, provided the ABPI is not below 0.8.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Intervention not possible; arteries normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Graduated compression stockings.

elim: For venous eczema flares, not symptoms of varicose veins.

steps.x: **A. Graduated compression stockings.** Stockings only when intervention unsuitable, and ABPI ≥0.8.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has painful varicose veins of his right leg and a healed venous ulcer. Duplex ultrasound shows reflux in a straight great saphenous vein with patent, competent deep veins. He is fit and wants treatment. His ABPI is 1.1.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line intervention?
questions.e: First-line interventional treatment is endothermal ablation (radiofrequency or endovenous laser ablation); foam sclerotherapy is second-line and surgery third-line.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.

clues: reflux in a straight great saphenous vein
steps.x: Suitable straight vein for a catheter.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Radiofrequency ablation.
**B. Radiofrequency ablation.** Endothermal ablation (RFA or EVLA) is first-line intervention.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has symptomatic varicose veins with great saphenous reflux on duplex. Endothermal ablation is unsuitable because the vein is very tortuous and a catheter cannot be passed. She is fit and wants treatment. Her ABPI is 1.0.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: When endothermal ablation is unsuitable, second-line is ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy (for example sodium tetradecyl sulfate).

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
First-line intervention is not possible: go second-line.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy.

elim: Only if all intervention is unsuitable.
A form of endothermal ablation, which is unsuitable.
She wants treatment for symptomatic veins.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy.** Second-line = foam sclerotherapy.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has symptomatic varicose veins with a large, very tortuous great saphenous vein and reflux at the saphenofemoral junction. Endothermal ablation is not possible and foam sclerotherapy failed twice. He is fit for a general anaesthetic. His ABPI is 1.1.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Surgical ligation and stripping is the third-line option when ablation and sclerotherapy are unsuitable or have failed.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
First- and second-line have failed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Saphenofemoral ligation and stripping.

elim: Only if all intervention is unsuitable.

steps.x: **E. Saphenofemoral ligation and stripping.** Third-line = surgical ligation and stripping.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with varicose veins has dry, itchy, scaly skin and brown pigmentation over both lower medial calves. There is no ulcer or infection. Her ABPI is 1.0 in both legs. Her temperature is 36.6°C and BP 132/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Emollients, graduated compression stockings and referral to vascular surgery
questions.e: Chronic venous insufficiency skin changes are managed with emollients and graduated compression stockings, and skin changes are referred to vascular surgery.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.

clues: dry, itchy, scaly skin and brown pigmentation
steps.x: Venous skin changes with safe arteries.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Emollients, graduated compression stockings and referral to vascular surgery.

elim: Skin changes need treatment and referral.
This is venous eczema, not fungal.

steps.x: **A. Emollients, graduated compression stockings and referral to vascular surgery.** Venous skin changes: emollient, stockings, vascular referral.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with varicose veins has a 3 cm tender, red, hard cord along a varicose tributary on her lower calf. Duplex ultrasound shows a short superficial thrombus 30 cm below the saphenofemoral junction with no deep vein thrombosis. Her temperature is 37.0°C. She has no history of peptic ulcer.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Low molecular weight heparin for 45 days
Surgical ligation of the saphenofemoral junction
questions.e: Superficial thrombophlebitis is treated with NSAIDs; LMWH is added only if it is extensive or near the saphenofemoral junction.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Short segment, far from the junction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral ibuprofen.

elim: For extensive thrombophlebitis or near the SFJ.
Not needed for a small distal thrombus.

steps.x: **C. Oral ibuprofen.** Small distal thrombophlebitis = NSAID.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with varicose veins has a 15 cm hard, red, tender cord along his great saphenous vein in the thigh. Duplex shows superficial thrombus extending to 2 cm from the saphenofemoral junction without deep vein thrombosis. He has no bleeding risk. His temperature is 37.1°C and eGFR 84 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: NSAID plus low molecular weight heparin
questions.e: Superficial thrombophlebitis is treated with NSAIDs; LMWH is added if it is extensive or near the saphenofemoral junction, because of the risk of spread into the deep system.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Extensive and close to the deep system.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: NSAID plus low molecular weight heparin.
**C. NSAID plus low molecular weight heparin.** Near the SFJ or extensive = add LMWH.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman has a few visible varicose veins on her left calf. She has no aching, swelling, bleeding, skin change or ulcer and is not troubled by them except that she dislikes how they look. Her BMI is 23 kg/m². Pulses are normal. She asks to be referred for surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure and advise conservative measures; do not refer
Refer to vascular surgery for ablation
questions.e: Varicose veins are not referred to vascular surgery for cosmetic reasons alone; referral is for bleeding, pain, thrombophlebitis, ulceration or severe impact on quality of life.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.

clues: no aching, swelling, bleeding, skin change or ulcer
steps.x: Cosmetic only: no referral criteria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reassure and advise conservative measures; do not refer.

elim: Not needed if no treatment is planned.
She has no symptoms to relieve.

steps.x: **D. Reassure and advise conservative measures; do not refer.** Not referred for cosmetic reasons alone.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with varicose veins presents to the emergency department after a vein over his right ankle burst while he was in the shower. It bled heavily but stopped with leg elevation and firm pressure. His Hb is 118 g/L. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 126/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate further management?
questions.e: Bleeding from varicose veins is a referral criterion for vascular surgery, after first aid with elevation and direct pressure.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.

clues: vein over his right ankle burst
stopped with leg elevation and firm pressure
steps.x: Bleeding has stopped; prevent recurrence.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Refer to vascular surgery.

elim: Bleeding is a referral criterion and can recur.
Not used for varicose vein bleeding.

steps.x: **C. Refer to vascular surgery.** Bleeding varicose vein = refer to vascular surgery.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has varicose veins of her left leg. When she lies down with the leg raised, the veins empty. When she stands, they refill within seconds from the groin downwards. She asks why her veins bulge only when she stands. Her BP is 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Blood refluxing distally under gravity through incompetent valves
Lymph collecting in the subcutaneous tissue
questions.e: Venous valves normally keep flow towards the heart; when incompetent, blood refluxes distally under gravity on standing, raising venous pressure and distending the veins.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: explain why the finding in the stem happens.

clues: refill within seconds from the groin downwards
steps.x: Filling from above means backwards flow.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Blood refluxing distally under gravity through incompetent valves.

elim: Gives a raised JVP and bilateral oedema.
DVT gives a swollen limb, not refilling from above.

steps.x: **B. Blood refluxing distally under gravity through incompetent valves.** Incompetent valves → reflux under gravity → venous hypertension.

questions.stem: A 49 year old shop worker with varicose veins finds the aching in her legs builds through each 10-hour shift standing at the till and settles by the next morning. She asks why standing makes it worse. Her BMI is 27 kg/m² and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Calf muscles stop working on standing
Gravity drives blood back through incompetent valves, raising venous pressure
Standing activates inflammatory cells in the veins
questions.e: When standing, gravity makes blood reflux distally through incompetent valves, raising venous pressure in the leg; this is why standing occupations are a risk factor and symptoms worsen through the day.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: explain why the finding in the stem happens.
Prolonged standing + gravity + leaky valves.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gravity drives blood back through incompetent valves, raising venous pressure.

elim: Arterial flow is helped by gravity.
The calf pump works with movement; standing still gives less pumping but the problem is the reflux.
Not the main mechanism of symptoms.

steps.x: **C. Gravity drives blood back through incompetent valves, raising venous pressure.** Standing raises venous pressure through leaky valves.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has had varicose veins for 35 years. Her lower calf skin has become hard and tight, and a shallow ulcer has now formed above the medial malleolus. Her ABPI is 1.0. A student asks how venous disease leads to an ulcer.
questions.q: Which is the most likely sequence?
o: Arterial occlusion causing focal tissue death
Sustained pressure over a bony prominence
Venous hypertension causing capillary damage, fibrosis and breakdown
questions.e: Raised venous pressure damages capillaries with red cell leakage; progressive fibrosis produces lipodermatosclerosis and eventually ulceration.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: explain why the finding in the stem happens.
Venous hypertension leads to fibrosis then ulceration.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Venous hypertension causing capillary damage, fibrosis and breakdown.

elim: Arterial ulcer mechanism; ABPI is normal.

steps.x: **E. Venous hypertension causing capillary damage, fibrosis and breakdown.** Venous hypertension → capillary damage → fibrosis (LDS) → ulcer.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has radiofrequency ablation of his great saphenous vein for symptomatic reflux. A catheter is passed into the vein under ultrasound and slowly withdrawn while energy is delivered. At 6 weeks duplex shows the treated vein is closed. He asks how this works.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Chemical damage to the endothelium by a sclerosant
Heat causing fibrosis and occlusion of the vein
questions.e: Endothermal ablation (laser or radiofrequency) uses heat energy to cause fibrosis and occlusion of the incompetent vein.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: explain why the finding in the stem happens.
Endothermal = heat.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Heat causing fibrosis and occlusion of the vein.

elim: Dissolves clot; the opposite of the aim.

steps.x: **B. Heat causing fibrosis and occlusion of the vein.** Ablation = heat → fibrosis → occlusion.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has endovenous laser ablation of her right great saphenous vein. She worries that closing a major leg vein will make her leg swell. Duplex before treatment showed patent, competent deep veins. At 3 months her leg is not swollen and her aching has gone.
questions.q: Which best explains why her leg does not swell?
o: Blood is redirected through the competent deep veins
The great saphenous vein recanalises within days
questions.e: After endothermal ablation, venous return is redirected through the competent deep veins, so occluding the superficial vein does not cause swelling.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: explain why the finding in the stem happens.
Deep veins carry most venous return anyway.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Blood is redirected through the competent deep veins.

elim: Arteries carry blood to tissue, not back.

steps.x: **B. Blood is redirected through the competent deep veins.** Ablation works because the deep veins take over.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man with varicose veins and peripheral arterial disease (ABPI 0.55) was given compression stockings by mistake. Within days his toes became painful, pale and cold, and a small ulcer formed over his heel. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the harm?
o: Allergic reaction to the stocking fabric
Deep vein thrombosis from the stocking
Venous pressure rising under the stocking
questions.e: Compression can worsen ischaemia in patients with significant arterial disease, which is why ABPI must be checked and stockings avoided if it is below 0.8.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: explain why the finding in the stem happens.
External pressure on already poorly perfused tissue.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Compression further reducing arterial perfusion.

elim: Gives a rash, not pale cold toes.
Not relevant to pale cold toes.

steps.x: **B. Compression further reducing arterial perfusion.** ABPI <0.8: compression worsens ischaemia.
